out.other_title: Key assumption: a human can coordinate copies of X to beat a single copy
out.rationale: Christiano et al. (2018) assume that a human can coordinate multiple copies of X to perform better than a single copy of X; the authors argue that stock amplification needs a human questioner able to produce strong consistency checks, a limitation debate avoids. It is a conceptual argument with no new data, and the authors present the two schemes as approximately equivalent once amplification adds an adversarial Questioner, so CHALLENGES: it shows a limit of the human-coordination assumption when strong subquestions are superhumanly hard to generate, rather than arguing that amplification is flawed.
out.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: Whether amplification's human-generated decomposition limits it relative to debate; holds for stock amplification with a supervised Questioner, not for variants with an adversarial Questioner

text: Comparing debate with Christiano et al.'s amplification, the authors argue that stock amplification relies on a human questioner: it assumes lying is harder than questioning a lie given a human judge and a human questioner, and shallow amplification is weaker than shallow debate when strong subquestions are superhumanly hard to generate or the branching factor is high. They add that this advantage goes away if the Questioner is trained adversarially via self play.
title: Irving et al.: stock amplification (Christiano et al.) needs humans to generate strong subquestions
